newsitem.title: UK: Market shrugs off talk of slow Cuba sugar shipment.
newsitem.headline: Market shrugs off talk of slow Cuba sugar shipment.

text.p: Cuba is reported to be lagging behind with this year's programme of sugar shipments but European traders mostly dismissed the talk as of little significance to world markets.

So far, loading at the island's ports is thought to have proceeded promptly and fewer problems have been seen this year with overseas deliveries of fuel, essential for the smooth progress of the harvest.
"There is plenty of sugar out there and it is being loaded all the time but perhaps people aren't getting quite so much as they would like," said one trader with a major London house.
"It's hard to tell, the Cubans tend to stretch themselves on their contracts."
In the latest monthly report published this week by Czarnikow Sugar, trade sources were quoted as saying Cuban raws shipments were behind last year.
"Shipments...are lagging behind last year's rate with some claiming the gap to be as much as 200,000 tonnes," it said.
But the exact discrepancy is unclear and a number of different figures are being floated around the market.

"There's a big range...it completely depends who you're asking. There's really a big difference. It's very hard to determine, especially how many Cubans (sugar) are going into Russia," another trader said.
Earlier this month brokers said Cuba could find itself in difficulties if the rainy season came early.
Some delays to the crop have been seen, partly due to the earlier damage wreaked by Hurricane Lili and also to operational hitches caused by a shortage of spare parts.
The harvest has also been hampered by the late arrivals of fertilizers, herbicides and pesticides and dry weather during the summer.

But other brokers said they had seen no problems with the shipments emerging from Cuba and cited unconfirmed talk that the state authorities had even asked for a couple of cargoes to be loaded early due to good supply.
Market sources said Russia was the key to the overall level of demand for Cuban raws and hence, to a certain extent, to the progress of shipments.
Much of last year's Cuban offtake came as a result of the bilateral oil-for-sugar deal, now in jeopardy after one of the two Russian partners pulled out after an acrimonious exchange with Havana.
"Last year they (Cuba) had a very large protocol with Alfa-Eko and Menatep...and it was in their interests to pump it out as quick as they could," said one broker.
He added that if the annual comparisons were taken over a longer period, shipments were still running well considering that the loading rate in 1996 had been unusually quick.
"I think the protocol talks have dragged on and nobody believes there'll even be one now -- it might just as well go through commercial channels," said Chris Pack, Czarnikow's senior analyst.
As a major world producer of raw sugar, Cuba could also opt to retain some of its output until demand and world physical prices pick up -- as Thailand is doing.
Cuba is not expected to issue details of its sugar shipments before June.
